title: How to Capture CBC Rubrics and Strands Without Excel
h1: How to Capture CBC Rubrics and Strands Without Excel
description: A practical, teacher-friendly way to capture CBC rubrics, strands and sub-strands without Excel — with a data model, a term setup and a class workflow.
author: SQUL Team
quickAnswer: To capture CBC rubrics and strands without Excel, stop building a grid of subjects and start keeping one row per learner, per sub-strand, per assessment event. Each row holds the learning area, strand, sub-strand, performance level, date, teacher and evidence. That structure can be filtered, moderated, exported for SBA and turned into a report card — a spreadsheet of merged cells cannot.
intro: **Quick answer:** the replacement for the class rubric workbook is not a prettier spreadsheet. It is a structured record: one row per learner, per sub-strand, per assessment event, with the level, date, teacher and evidence attached. This guide shows how to capture CBC rubrics and strands without Excel, set the record up for a Kenyan class, capture in the classroom without adding a second job, and keep it clean enough for moderation and reporting. For the whole-school picture, start with the [complete guide to CBC assessment management](/blog/cbc-assessment-management-complete-guide).

Most teachers do not abandon Excel because they love spreadsheets. They abandon it because the workbook asks them to hold three different things at once: the curriculum structure, the learner list, and the evidence. When a strand changes, a learner transfers or a parent disputes a level, the workbook has no way to explain itself.

The good news is that the fix is small. You do not need to digitise every lesson. You need a record that answers four questions for every level: **who**, **which sub-strand**, **what evidence**, and **who recorded it**. Everything else is a view.

sections.heading: Why the class rubric workbook feels right — until it doesn't

blocks.text: A workbook is familiar, offline and fast to start. For one class, one term and one teacher, it can work. The problems appear when the record has to survive a second teacher, a second stream or a second term.

items: **Columns become the curriculum.** A teacher adds a column for every task, and by week eight the sheet is 40 columns wide with no consistent definition of what each column measures.
**Merged cells hide learners.** A merged cell for a strand looks tidy on screen, but filters, counts and exports silently drop rows.
**Free-text levels drift.** One teacher types EE, another types Exceeding, another types 4. The school cannot count or compare any of them.
**The evidence lives elsewhere.** The photo of the project is on a phone, the rubric note is in an exercise book, and the level is in the sheet. Three places, no link.
**There is no history.** When a level is corrected, the old value disappears. Nobody can explain what changed or why.

blocks.title: Excel is a calculation tool, not a records system
blocks.text: A records system enforces the shape of the data: one learner, one sub-strand, one level, one date. Excel lets anyone change the shape at any time — which is exactly why it is hard to trust at reporting time.
CBC assessment language is precise, and the precision is useful. If teachers use the same terms in the same way, moderation becomes a conversation rather than an argument.

blocks.caption: The CBC record vocabulary, with a Mathematics example.
rows: The subject or broad area of learning
A broad organising theme within the learning area
A specific cluster of learning outcomes inside a strand
What the learner should know or do
The descriptor of how well the outcome was demonstrated
The task, observation or product behind the level
The occasion on which evidence was collected

blocks.text: A report card only needs the learning area and an overall level. But an overall level is a **summary** of sub-strand evidence, not a separate judgement. If the sub-strand record is thin, the summary is a guess with a nice font.

sections.heading: The one-row rule: structure beats decoration

blocks.text: The core design decision is simple: **one row per learner, per sub-strand, per assessment event**. A learner assessed on three sub-strands in one task creates three rows. A class of 45 learners assessed on four sub-strands creates 180 rows — which sounds like a lot until you realise the workbook already contains the same information, just spread across a grid nobody can filter.

blocks.caption: The same evidence, stored as rows instead of a wide grid.

blocks.text: Rows look less impressive on a screen, but they do something a wide grid cannot: they let the school ask questions. Which learners are missing a level for Fractions? Which sub-strands has this class not assessed? Which teacher's ME rates look different from the rest of the stream? Those are reporting questions, and they need a structure, not a layout.

blocks.caption: Illustrative view: one learner row across four sub-strands, with a live count of what is still missing. The grid is a view of the rows, not the record itself.

sections.heading: Set up the term in six steps

blocks.text: Do the setup once, before teaching starts. A school that sets up in week one spends the rest of the term capturing; a school that sets up in week ten spends the rest of the term reconstructing.

items.title: Load the learners
items.text: Import the class list with UPI, admission number and stream. Check for duplicates before anything else — a duplicate learner is the most expensive error to unwind.

items.title: Load the curriculum map
items.text: Add the learning areas, strands and sub-strands for the term. This is the school's agreed map, not each teacher's personal interpretation.

items.title: Agree the scale
items.text: Decide whether the school reports EE/ME/AE/BE or the eight-point EE1–BE2 scale. Use one scale for capture and map it to the report card later.

items.title: Plan the evidence
items.text: For each sub-strand, name the task, project or observation that will produce evidence. A sub-strand with no planned task is a sub-strand that will be filled in at the last minute.

items.title: Assign the teachers
items.text: Match each learning area and stream to a teacher. If two teachers share a class, agree who owns the final level.

items.title: Publish the calendar
items.text: Give teachers the capture windows and the lock date. The lock date is what makes the report card possible.

sections.heading: Capture in class without adding a second job

blocks.text: The biggest reason digital capture fails is that it becomes an evening data-entry shift. The rule is to capture at the point of evidence, in the smallest useful unit.

items: **Use a phone, not a laptop.** A teacher moving around a classroom will not open a spreadsheet; they will tap a learner and a level.
**Capture the exception first.** Mark the learners who are EE or BE explicitly, then confirm the majority as ME. It is faster and it surfaces the learners who need support.
**Attach one piece of evidence.** A photo of a project, a scanned rubric or a short note is enough. You do not need a portfolio for every sub-strand.
**Batch by task, not by learner.** After a task, capture all 45 learners for the same sub-strand while the standard is still fresh in your mind.
**Never transcribe twice.** If the level is entered on paper first, the paper is the source and the digital record is a copy. Choose one source of truth and stick to it.

blocks.title: The 90-second rule
blocks.text: If capturing a class set of levels takes longer than 90 seconds, the tool or the setup is wrong. Teachers will not sustain a workflow that feels like a second job — no matter how good the report card looks.

sections.heading: The four levels and the eight-point scale

blocks.text: CBC reports four performance descriptors. National reporting subdivides each into two, creating an eight-point scale. Schools need to decide which one their report card uses — and make sure the capture screen uses the same one.

blocks.caption: Performance descriptors, with the eight-point subdivision.
rows: The learner applies the competency independently and beyond the expected level
The learner demonstrates the competency as expected
The learner is developing the competency with support
The learner needs substantial support to demonstrate the competency

blocks.text: The two sub-levels are not a way to rank learners more precisely. They are a way to record movement — a learner moving from AE2 to ME1 is showing progress even though the descriptor has only changed by one step. Use them to tell that story, not to create a league table.

blocks.title: Agree the scale before the term, not after
blocks.text: A school that captures EE/ME/AE/BE all term and then tries to print EE1–BE2 report cards has created a conversion problem for itself. Decide once, document it, and map any historical data deliberately.

sections.heading: Moderation without a meeting for every learner

blocks.text: Moderation is the difference between a record and a rumour. It does not require a meeting about every learner. It requires a sample, a common standard and a short conversation.

items: **Sample across streams.** Pick three learners from each stream — one EE, one ME, one AE — and compare the evidence behind the levels.
**Cross-mark one task.** Give two teachers the same five pieces of work and compare their levels before they capture the rest.
**Anchor the standard with examples.** Keep one annotated example per level for each strand. New teachers then have something concrete to compare against.
**Record the moderation.** A short note — date, strand, sample size, decision — is enough to show that the school checked.
**Fix the standard, not the numbers.** If two teachers disagree, the answer is usually a clearer task or rubric, not an instruction to lower everyone's level.

sections.heading: Moving the current workbook into the new record

blocks.text: You do not have to abandon the current term's data. Migrate it deliberately, and treat the migration as a data-cleaning exercise rather than a copy-and-paste.

items.title: Freeze the workbook
items.text: Make one read-only copy and name it with the term and date. From this point, nobody edits it.

items.title: List the learners
items.text: Extract the unique learner list and reconcile it against the admission register. Fix duplicates and missing UPIs first.

items.title: Reshape the grid
items.text: Turn each subject column into a learning area row, and each task column into an assessment event. This is the step a spreadsheet cannot do for you.

items.title: Normalise the levels
items.text: Map every variant — EE, E, Exceeding, 4, 75% — to one scale. Record the mapping so the school can explain it later.

items.title: Validate before importing
items.text: Check that every learner has a level for every assessed sub-strand, and that no level sits outside the scale.

items.title: Lock and archive
items.text: Import, spot-check 10 learners against the workbook, then archive the workbook as the evidence of the migration.

items: Every learner has a unique record and a UPI before capture begins.
The term's strands and sub-strands are agreed and loaded once.
One performance scale is in use across all streams.
Every sub-strand has a planned task or observation.
Teachers can capture from a phone in under 90 seconds per class set.
Each level can be traced to a date, a task and a teacher.
A moderation sample has been checked across streams.
The record can be filtered by learner, strand, stream and teacher.
The term can be locked without losing the ability to correct errors.
A backup exists outside the teacher's laptop.

blocks.title: The test of a good record
blocks.text: Hand the record to a teacher who did not create it and ask them to explain one learner's level. If they can do it in under a minute, the structure is working.

SQUL stores CBC assessment as structured rows against the learner, learning area, strand and sub-strand, rather than as a subject grid. Teachers capture levels on a phone, the DOS can see what is missing by stream, and the term record feeds report cards and SBA exports.

items: **Strands and sub-strands** loaded once per term and shared across streams.
**Performance levels** captured against the learner, with date, teacher and evidence.
**Moderation views** that compare streams and flag missing sub-strands.
**A locked term record** that report cards and KNEC exports read from.
**Role-based access and daily backups**, so the record is not dependent on one laptop.

faqs.question: Do I need to record every sub-strand for every learner?
faqs.answer: You need enough evidence to support the level you report. In practice that means every sub-strand you assessed should have a recorded level, and every learning area reported should be backed by sub-strand evidence. Sub-strands you did not assess should not be invented at term end.

faqs.question: Should I use EE/ME/AE/BE or the eight-point scale?
faqs.answer: Use the scale your report card and KNEC reporting require. The four descriptors are the school-facing summary; the eight-point EE1–BE2 scale adds a sub-level for finer progress. Decide before the term and use one scale for capture, mapping only when you generate a report.

faqs.question: Can teachers capture rubrics on a phone?
faqs.answer: Yes, and they should. A phone-based capture screen that takes a few taps per learner is far more likely to be used at the point of evidence than a laptop spreadsheet opened in the evening.

faqs.question: What evidence should be attached to a level?
faqs.answer: One traceable artefact is enough: a photo of a project, a scanned task, a short observation note or a rubric sheet. The point is to be able to explain the level later, not to build a portfolio for every sub-strand.

faqs.question: Can I migrate the current term's Excel data?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you freeze the workbook, reconcile the learner list, reshape the grid into one row per learner per sub-strand, normalise the level values and validate before importing. Archive the original workbook as evidence of the migration.
